stem: In the indirect method, why is depreciation added back to profit before tax?

options.content: It reduced profit but did not use any cash
options.rationale: Correct: it is a non-cash expense.

options.content: It is a cash receipt from customers
options.rationale: Depreciation is not a receipt of any kind.

options.content: It increases the bank balance at the year end
options.rationale: Depreciation has no effect on the bank balance.

options.content: It is paid to the supplier at the year end
options.rationale: No payment is made for depreciation.

explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset over its life; the cash left when the asset was bought, so it is added back.

stem: An increase in inventory during the year is treated in the reconciliation of profit before tax to cash as:

options.content: a deduction, because cash was tied up in stock
options.rationale: Correct: more cash has been spent on inventory.

options.content: an addition, because assets have increased
options.rationale: More inventory means less cash.

options.content: an addition, because profit is higher
options.rationale: Inventory does not change profit in this adjustment.

options.content: no adjustment, because inventory is not cash
options.rationale: Changes in working capital are always adjusted.

explanation: An increase in inventory means that cash was used to buy goods that have not yet been sold, so it is deducted.

stem: An increase in trade payables during the year is treated in the reconciliation as:

options.content: a deduction, because liabilities have increased
options.rationale: More payables means cash was retained.

options.content: an addition to profit before tax in the statement of profit or loss
options.rationale: It is an adjustment in the cash flow statement only.

options.content: an addition, because cash was kept in the business
options.rationale: Correct: suppliers have financed part of the purchases.

options.content: a deduction, because suppliers have been paid
options.rationale: A rise in payables means suppliers have not been paid.

explanation: Paying suppliers later keeps cash in the business, so an increase in payables is added.

stem: Profit before tax was US\$46,500 after charging depreciation of US\$9,300, finance costs of US\$2,100 and a loss on disposal of US\$1,200. What is the operating profit before working capital changes?

options.rationale: The loss on disposal has been deducted instead of added back.
The finance costs have not been added back.
Depreciation has been deducted instead of added back.

hints: All three items reduced profit but are not operating cash flows.

stem: A profit on disposal of a non-current asset is shown in the reconciliation of profit before tax to cash generated from operations as:

options.content: an addition, with the proceeds shown in operating activities
options.rationale: A profit is removed because it is not an operating cash flow.

options.content: a deduction, with the proceeds shown in investing activities
options.rationale: Correct: the cash is an investing flow.

options.content: a deduction, with the proceeds shown in financing activities
options.rationale: Sale of an asset is an investing activity.

options.content: no adjustment, because disposals do not affect cash
options.rationale: The proceeds are a cash inflow in investing activities.

explanation: The profit is deducted from profit before tax so that it is not counted twice; the proceeds appear in investing activities.
hints: Where are the sale proceeds shown?

stem: During the year inventory fell by US\$3,400, trade receivables rose by US\$5,800 and trade payables rose by US\$2,200. What is the net effect of the working capital changes on cash?

options.content: An increase of US\$200
options.rationale: The receivables increase is larger than the other two changes combined.

options.content: A decrease of US\$11,400
options.rationale: All three changes have been deducted.

options.content: An increase of US\$11,400
options.rationale: All three changes have been added.

options.content: A decrease of US\$200

explanation: Inventory fall +3,400; receivables rise -5,800; payables rise +2,200; total -200.
hints: Release of cash is positive, tying up cash is negative.

stem: A company's profit before tax was US\$40,000 but cash generated from operations was only US\$12,000. Which is the most likely explanation?

options.content: Depreciation was too high
options.rationale: Depreciation is added back, so it would raise cash generated, not lower it.

options.content: Trade payables increased by a large amount
options.rationale: That would increase cash generated.

options.content: Inventory and receivables rose sharply
options.rationale: Correct: profit was recorded but cash was tied up.

options.content: A profit on disposal was made
options.rationale: A profit on disposal is deducted but is not the main reason.

explanation: Growth in inventory and receivables ties up cash, so profit converts to cash only in part.

stem: Tax payable was US\$4,800 at the start of the year and US\$6,300 at the end. The tax charge for the year was US\$13,100. How much tax was paid?

options.rationale: The charge is not the cash paid.
The opening and closing balances have been reversed.
The closing payable has been added instead of deducted.

explanation: Tax paid = opening payable + charge - closing payable = 4,800 + 13,100 - 6,300 = 11,600.

stem: A loss on the disposal of a non-current asset is added back to profit before tax when calculating cash generated from operations.
explanation: True. The loss reduced profit but is not an operating cash flow; the proceeds appear in investing activities.

stem: Dividends paid are deducted in arriving at cash generated from operations.
explanation: False. Dividends paid are a financing cash flow and are not part of cash generated from operations.
hints: Which activity do dividends belong to?

stem: Match each item to its adjustment when reconciling profit before tax to cash generated from operations.
explanation: Non-cash expenses are added back, increases in working capital assets are deducted, profits on disposal are deducted and increases in payables are added.

stem: Complete the sentences about the order of the statement.

payload.template: Interest paid and tax paid are deducted {{blank:a}} cash generated from operations. Dividends paid are shown in {{blank:b}} activities.

explanation: Cash generated from operations is before interest and tax paid; dividends paid are a financing flow.

stem: Name the method of presenting operating cash flows that starts with profit before tax.
explanation: The indirect method starts with profit and adjusts it; the direct method lists cash receipts and payments.

stem: Profit before tax was US\$38,900 after charging depreciation of US\$7,600 and finance costs of US\$1,850. Inventory rose by US\$4,100, trade receivables rose by US\$2,900 and trade payables rose by US\$1,300. Calculate cash generated from operations.
explanation: 38,900 + 7,600 + 1,850 - 4,100 - 2,900 + 1,300 = 42,650. Ignoring the working capital changes gives 48,350.
workedSolution: 1. 38,900 + 7,600 + 1,850 - 4,100 - 2,900 + 1,300 = 42,650. Ignoring the working capital changes gives 48,350.
hints: Add back depreciation and finance costs, then adjust for working capital.

stem: Income tax payable was US\$3,300 at the start of the year and US\$2,900 at the end. The income tax expense for the year was US\$8,700. Calculate the income tax paid.
Retained earnings were US\$33,400 at the start of the year and US\$41,250 at the end. Dividends paid were US\$9,800. Calculate the profit for the year.
explanation: Profit for the year = 41,250 - 33,400 + 9,800 = 17,650. Using only the change in retained earnings gives 7,850.
workedSolution: 1. Profit for the year = 41,250 - 33,400 + 9,800 = 17,650. Using only the change in retained earnings gives 7,850.

stem: Explain why a company can make a profit and still have a falling bank balance.

points.description: Profit includes sales made on credit, and the cash has not yet been received
Cash may be used to buy non-current assets, pay loans, tax and dividends, none of which reduces profit before tax

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Credit sales are in profit but not yet in the bank. Cash may also go on new assets, loan repayments, tax and dividends, which do not reduce profit before tax.

explanation: One mark for each reason.

stem: Explain how an increase in trade receivables affects the cash generated from operations.

points.description: Sales are recorded in profit when made, but the cash is received only when customers pay
An increase in receivables means that less cash was received than the sales recorded
It is therefore deducted from profit before tax in the reconciliation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sales appear in profit when made, but if receivables rise, customers have not yet paid for part of them. Less cash has been received than profit suggests, so the increase is deducted.

explanation: One mark for each step of the argument.
hints: Compare the cash received with the sales recorded.

stem: A company reports a profit before tax of US\$80,000 but cash generated from operations of US\$15,000. Suggest reasons and advise the directors.

points.description: Large increases in inventory and trade receivables tie up cash
Fewer purchases may have been paid for late; if payables fell, cash left the business
Because profit includes unpaid sales, the company may find it hard to pay its own bills
Advice: tighten credit control, reduce excess inventory and negotiate longer supplier terms

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The most likely causes are large rises in inventory and receivables, and a fall in payables. The company may struggle to pay its bills. The directors should collect receivables faster, reduce inventory and ask suppliers for longer credit.

explanation: One mark each for two causes, the consequence and the advice.
hints: Which three working capital items could absorb the cash?

stem: Zaka Maize Mills Ltd made a profit before tax of US\$63,400 for the year ended 31 December 2025, after charging depreciation of US\$18,750 and finance costs of US\$4,200 (paid in full) and after crediting a profit of US\$2,350 on the disposal of a machine. During the year inventory rose by US\$6,450, trade receivables fell by US\$3,150 and trade payables rose by US\$1,900. Income tax paid was US\$16,700.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the operating profit before working capital changes.
parts.explanation: 63,400 + 18,750 + 4,200 - 2,350 = 84,000. The profit on disposal is deducted.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 63,400 + 18,750 + 4,200 - 2,350 = 84,000. The profit on disposal is deducted.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the net effect of the working capital changes on cash. Enter a decrease as a negative number.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the cash generated from operations.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the net cash from operating activities.

explanation: This item tests the reconciliation of profit before tax to net operating cash.
hints: A profit on disposal is deducted.
Interest and tax paid come after cash generated from operations.
